absent: Lock implementation, contention behavior, and interrupt safety beyond acquisition ordering are not shown.
Page table entry bit layout and protection attribute encodings beyond ownership and annotation discriminants are not shown.
VM creation, handle allocation, reference counting details, and teardown beyond dying reclamation are not shown.
Timer, vector, and system register runtime emulation semantics beyond initialization are not shown.
Memory range table construction and host mapping protection values are not shown.
Scheduling, preemption, and cross CPU visibility bounds for hypervisor calls are not shown.

findings.text: Host to hypervisor donation and the reverse transfer each expose a range transfer contract keyed by start frame plus length. Success moves stewardship of the whole interval between protection domains while failure leaves prior stewardship unchanged and reports an error status.

A locked helper centralizes host second stage ownership changes. One path restores host accessibility with host memory protections and marks host stewardship, while the other path records hypervisor ownership through metadata without restoring access.

Virtual CPU creation exposes a handle based instantiation contract. The caller supplies a VM identifier plus host side descriptors and a donor address. The implementation maps private state, resolves the VM, initializes generic and architecture state, publishes the record, and releases private state on any failure.

Poison fault inspection exposes a query that reports whether the currently faulting guest mapping is in the poisoned annotation state. It only answers for lower level data or instruction aborts that represent translation faults and rejects other trap conditions.

Guest page reclamation exposes forced, dying VM, and per frame entry points. Forced reclamation targets a host physical address and always poisons before returning it. Dying VM reclamation gates on a dying flag and delegates to a guest frame routine that handles owned and shared owned cases distinctly.

Supporting exports provide stage two annotation with caller supplied annotation bits, one time protected identification register initialization, and a predicate that reports whether a physical address belongs to known memory.

Hypervisor call shims translate host register state into protected operations. Each shim extracts operands from fixed argument registers, converts host addresses into hypervisor usable form where needed, invokes the corresponding operation, and returns status through the primary result register.

Donation in either direction validates the frame interval before acquiring protection state and requires complementary stewardship views. One side must show owned while the other shows empty, with the hypervisor to host direction additionally requiring a quiescent reference count. Restoration to host additionally requires the interval to lie in ordinary memory.

Donated and reclaimed memory is sanitized to prevent cross domain leakage. Freshly mapped donor regions are cleared before use, released regions are cleared before return, reclaimed guest contents are cleared through a temporary mapping, and cache maintenance to point of coherency precedes ownership transfer.

New virtual CPU state links host and hypervisor records through pinned shared memory. Identity and control flags are sampled once from the host, execution starts stopped, timer offsets for non protected guests alias host VM timer storage, and vector state length is clamped to the lesser of host request and hypervisor support with validation before pinning.

Trap controls start from a common guest baseline adjusted for platform capabilities such as virtualization host extensions, reliability, writeback, address width, and pointer authentication. Non protected guests inherit extended control from host while protected guests undergo feature validation and then enable trapping of identification, debug, performance, and optional architecture facilities when the corresponding feature is absent.

Identification register state is initialized exactly once per VM. Non protected guests copy host values only after host initialization, protected guests compute values from host capabilities masked by per field maxima with special handling for debug and memory model registers and zero for unhandled encodings, iterating only the wide address range.

Publication of a new virtual CPU requires an index within the created count and an empty slot. The initialized record becomes visible to the load path through ordered release publication only after full initialization.

Guest mappings are accepted only when leaf lookup succeeds, the entry is neither poisoned nor invalid, resides at the final table level, and refers to allowed memory. Host donation metadata is accepted only for invalid entries of donation type owned by guests, with handle resolution failure and host owned or shared states reported as retryable rather than fatal.

Range donation acquires host protection before hypervisor protection and releases in reverse order, holding both across state verification and mutation so the two views change atomically from the perspective of concurrent donors.

VM table serialization nests outside host and guest protection serialization. Creation and forced reclamation hold the table lock across lookup and mutation, per VM and host reclamation hold host outside guest, poison queries hold only guest, and protected identification initialization asserts table ownership.

A hypervisor VM record aggregates a generic VM object, a table of hypervisor virtual CPU pointers indexed by guest position, a reference to host VM state, and a guest second stage table. Each hypervisor virtual CPU embeds a generic virtual CPU plus a link to its host counterpart and shares address space roots with its VM.

Architecture state observed in this lane includes second stage root, control flags, power state, trap controls for execution and debug, extended control, vector length and vector storage, and per VM identification storage with an initialized marker. Timer offsets for non protected guests are indirections into host VM timer data rather than owned values.

A physical interval cycles among host owned, hypervisor owned, guest associated, and empty views. Host donation moves an empty hypervisor view to owned while marking host as hypervisor owned. Reverse donation clears the hypervisor view and restores host owned. Guest reclamation unmaps the guest view, optionally poisons contents, and then restores host owned.

Virtual CPU slots progress from absent to initialized to published, with failure unwinding pinning and private mappings. Identification storage progresses from uninitialized to initialized once. Reclamation of a guest frame is permitted only while its VM is marked dying, and poisoned annotations represent a terminal reclaimed marker that later lookups report distinctly.

Several unexpected conditions are recorded as warnings while execution continues with best effort completion, including mapping creation, ownership updates, unmapping size mismatch, physical address divergence, and table level mismatch. Callers cannot rely on warnings to prevent state mutation.

Cross domain handling avoids exposing guest access patterns by re deriving fault addresses from hardware registers rather than trusting host supplied values, avoids cache maintenance elision by forcing maintenance to point of coherency on reclaim, and requires ordered publication plus single sampling of host mutable fields to limit check versus use races.

Status reporting distinguishes invalid arguments, missing tables or mappings, busy shared pinning, permission violations, oversize mappings, hardware poison, memory faults, and retryable races. Poisoned guest lookups and already force reclaimed frames use dedicated poison indication that some callers normalize to success for reference release.

Protection state uses distinct owned, empty, shared owned, and shared borrowed markers together with distinct host, hypervisor, and guest ownership identities and a donation annotation type plus a poisoned annotation type to discriminate unmapped encodings.

Second stage annotation rejects out of mask annotation bits and rejects empty or locked annotation categories, then performs a table walk that forces leaf creation and records the supplied annotation combined with the requested category.
